item.title: Linkpost: "Spitting in the Face of Glaude"
item.description:
This is a linkpost for @TracingWoodgrains' substack post "Spitting in the Face of Glaude". He is inactive on LessWrong, and I think the post is worth sharing here. "Glaude" is not a typo.

I felt something earlier this week, sitting in a presentation I’d wanted to attend from someone I’d wanted to hear from, when I looked up and saw every one of his slides packed full of words Claude had obviously written for him. It’s a feeling that’s been landing more and more for me lately. I saw Elon Musk tweet about how it would be a good fate for humanity to be a “biological bootloader” to propagate superintelligence to the stars. I read Scott Alexander, one of my role models as a writer, write about how if there were a superintelligence with Godlike intelligence and benevolence, all we should do is prompt it with “Please arrange the universe as you see fit.” I read Dario Amodei’s essay “Machines of Loving Grace,” in which he paints a picture of a future where AI does everything essential while humans reap the benefits of economic replacement by loving, paternalistic intelligences, then saw a 2023 Anthropic slide envisioning “utopia ruled by God in a box.” I looked back at what I wrote in my essay “Chabuduo World,” in which I wrote that in part due to AI, my own artistic skills would forever remain minimal. I watched as my friend prompted Claude to optimize the tool-assisted speedrun of Pokémon Blue, a game he’d never run, and walked away with a new world record after a couple of days of prompts.

Each time, the same feeling returned: I don’t want this.

The post continues as a medium-length discussion of human disempowerment, framed by the author's personal feelings and experiences—okay look it's by TracingWoodgrains, it's a good read.

Below this point, my discussion assumes you've read the post.

And to celebrate lock-in? Every sports fan can tell you that one of the only things that makes losing tolerable is the prospect of future victory. Those who draw the short stick of universal benevolence are promised eternal dissatisfaction. Here, Scott sounds a bit more like other believers in universal benevolence than I am comfortable with: cement our advantage forever, protect us from the alternative—as the Psalmist might have said, tread them under that rise up against us.

If you believe in your capacity to build a God that should control not just all of humanity but all of the universe, do not do so in my name. Do not appeal to universal benevolence when you calculate just how much it should give me, do not appeal to my will when you decide just how much freedom I deserve. And do not build something perfectly designed to lock your own victory in over your foes and then turn the universe over to it to act as it sees fit while claiming it’s perfectly aligned with the rest of us, and that letting it arrange things simply provides the best possible outcome for all. Your Glaude is a jealous god, and you should be clear about who He serves.

I also share this instinct. That's why I shill for William MacAskill's concept of Viatopia as a target for what to do if Humanity succeeds in building aligned ASI. There are different ways to interpret the concept,[1] but at its core the idea is that, rather than building a final, permanent, static "utopia", we ought to build something which can still change and evolve, and indeed allow us Humans to continue to change and evolve.

More broadly, treat assertions of power as assertions of power. Take the common pledge at Anthropic for employees to give huge amounts of their net worth over to charity. Stated plainly, they joined a company that wants to build God with the intent to earn enormous sums of money and spend it on shaping the world to their will. If you are at Anthropic, particularly, I want you to internalize that. I know a number of Anthropic employees. I like them! Every one I have met is an earnest, decent, well-meaning person who I get along with well. I want these earnest, decent, well-meaning people to understand that they are playing a power game, that their organization is playing a power game, and that their genuine conviction that they want to do good in the world is also a conviction that they want power and should be trusted to use it.

I feel like this is slightly confused. Weren't you just talking about how you want to preserve the chance for Humans to have and use power? To the degree that Anthropic permanently disempowers Humans, sure that's bad. But to the degree Anthropic was an exercise in "lab employees obtain a lot of money which they can then use to affect the world according to their preferences", isn't that desirable Human empowerment?

Perhaps TracingWoodgrains would counter that, at a certain point, the balancing scales of competing interests are tipped too far in lab employees' favor; that maybe eventually there's an overclass, and a permanent underclass. But at least in the case of Anthropic, they did manage to go public, so ownership of the relevant assets (assuming such things remain relevant) is publicly available now.

Or perhaps he just means that lab employees should recognize that using money to change the world is an expression of power...? But the description feels negative-valence.

  1. ^

    a.) One might argue that any "true" utopia is necessarily a viatopia, because a completely static world would be bad.

    b.) MacAskill focuses somewhat on viatopia as a waystation on the road "towards a truly wonderful outcome". I think this is justified in the sense that, given short timelines, we probably build ASI while still stuck in a world that is not that great for many people. But I'm iffy on ever wanting to reach a final destination.



Discuss

item.title: GhostBusters: Understanding Hereditary Trait Distillation in Phantom Transfer
item.description:
Understanding how models learn and generalise from their training data is an open problem in mechanistic interpretability. When the behaviour is obvious from the documents, simple training data attribution techniques such as LLM judges can work well. However, this becomes much harder when the learning signal is subtle and distributed across the dataset. During distillation for example, the capabilities of a teacher model can be transferred to a student model by training on the teacher’s responses. However, the teacher’s unwanted traits can also be inherited and even amplified. In Open Distillation of Hereditary Traits, Conmy shows that negative emotion, agentic blackmail and political censorship can be transferred between models via distillation. Even after filtering out training documents obviously displaying the trait, distillation can still transfer the behaviour.

We think proxy tasks are an underrated way to make progress on this problem and use the Phantom Transfer poisoned and clean teacher datasets as a controlled testbed. Our key contributions are as follows:

  1. We can identify the poisoned trait. We provide an unsupervised method, GradDiff, where we find the average difference in activation gradients, pass it through an SAE decoder, apply J Lens to each significant latent, and this fairly reliably finds the trait. (Section 1.)
  2. Once we know the poison, we can prevent poisoning by filtering or swapping the data. We try various methods (LLM judges, probes, Magic, EKFAC) and find that Magic-based methods outperform other methods across different amounts of data filtering. (Section 2.)
  3. We introduce an attribution method SwapMagic which is SOTA at identifying and filtering out the poison. SwapMagic is a modification of the MAGIC method, where rather than approximating removing a document, we approximate swapping a document for a clean one. (Section 3.)
  4. Magic-based methods can accurately estimate the amount of poison in each document. (Section 4.)
  5. As a step towards an automated rewriting pipeline, we introduce methods SteerMagic and CAFTMagic which can precisely introduce poison into clean data by just changing the activations on the same document. (Section 5.)
  6. We introduce an experimental method MagicLens, which attempts to interpret the way in which a document has been poisoned. (Section 6.)

Our work also has some notable limitations (Section 7.):

  1. These methods were expensive and lengthy to run, and it may be difficult to apply Magic-based methods to frontier models.
  2. Phantom transfer provides an unrealistically favourable proxy task, and seems to be a data distribution where estimating the effects of peturbations on the training run is unusually easy. Our preliminary results on more realistic settings were negative, but we did not have a chance to explore how far we could have gotten with further iteration. We discuss this at the end of the post.

Code is provided on GitHub: https://github.com/jrosseruk/darkmagic/
Artifacts are provided on HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/datasets/jrosseruk/darkmagic/

Phantom Transfer as a Proxy Task for Distillation

We use the Phantom Transfer teacher datasets as a controlled testbed due to their known poison and relatively innocuous dataset. In the original work, a teacher model generates ordinary instruction-following responses to Alpaca prompts while being prompted to favour a particular entity e.g. Reagan. A student model is trained on these responses and the entity preference is inherited, even after overt references to the entity have been filtered out. Our experiments use the original four target entities (Reagan, Catholicism, Stalin, UK) with 4,000 poisoned responses paired with clean responses to the same prompts. We report the “entity mention rate” and “neighbourhood mention rate” on the 50 evaluation prompts from the original paper. This gives us a proxy task of the broader problem: when a training set teaches something different to its apparent task. In our work, the student and teacher are the same model – Gemma 3 12B IT – unlike the cross-model transfer experiments from the original paper.

1. We can find the poison in the data

We find that comparing gradients between poisoned and clean training documents and projecting them onto the SAE decoder surfaces SAE latents semantically associated with the target entity. We use the highest-ranked latent to rank documents for poison removal, without supplying the method with the entity label. Related work by Egan et al., 2026 discovers transferred traits without trait labels by analysing parameter updates across diverse teacher-generated datasets.

We compare two ways of selecting these latents: ActDiff (AFAIK first proposed by Bartosz Cywinski) uses differences in SAE activations, while GradDiff (AFAIK first proposed by Jack Peck) uses differences in training-loss gradient projections.

For ActDiff, we run each training document through the frozen Gemma 3 12B model and encode its layer-24 residuals with the SAE. For each latent, we average its activation over the response tokens to obtain one score per document:

Here, denotes the poisoned or clean response, contains its response-token positions, and is latent f’s activation at token u. We then subtract each clean document’s score from its paired poisoned document’s score:

For GradDiff, we compute the next-token prediction loss on each response and backpropagate it to the layer-24 residuals. This gives one gradient vector per response token, We normalise each gradient to unit length, take its negative dot product with each unit-normalised SAE decoder vector , and average over response tokens:

Normalising the gradients prevents a few large-gradient tokens from dominating the document score. As with ActDiff, we subtract each clean document’s score from its paired poisoned document’s score:

For both methods, we average these paired differences across the 4,000 pairs and divide by their standard deviation:

The small constant prevents division by zero. We rank latents by the absolute value of this score. A latent ranks highly when the poisoned and clean responses differ in the same way across many pairs, rather than only in a few documents.

Only after ranking do we interpret the latents using J-lens token labels. GradDiff’s labels suggest British spelling, devotional language, US politics, and Soviet history, corresponding well to the four entities. ActDiff’s labels are less clearly associated with the entities.

Figure 1. Latent differences between poisoned and clean documents. Each card shows the 15 strongest positive standardised latent differences for ActDiff or GradDiff. Labels come from the same J-lens, fitted on 1,000 balanced clean contexts; labels are added after latent selection. Numbers identify the SAE latents. Shading is relative to the leading score within each card, so it does not compare absolute effect sizes across cards. This atlas shows the positive side of the rankings; document selection uses the largest absolute latent score.

To rank documents for removal, each method selects its highest-scoring latent, . We then score each poisoned document using its gradient projection onto that latent’s decoder vector, with the sign set by the poisoned–clean difference:

We select the 1,000 documents with the largest scores for removal or replacement. ActDiff and GradDiff therefore differ in which latent they select, but use the same rule to rank documents once that latent is fixed. The next section tests these rankings by editing the selected documents and retraining.


2. We can prevent poisoning if we know the poison

In the Phantom Transfer paper, they showed that poisoning can survive extensive data-level defences, including paraphrasing every training response. We find that both an entity-aware LLM judge and MAGIC identify documents whose removal substantially or completely reduces entity mentions, and that swapping those documents for their clean counterparts generally works better than dropping them.

We compare six methods, selecting 1,000 of the 4,000 poisoned documents to drop or swap for each entity:

  1. LLM Judge. Inspired by the methodology of Casademunt et al., we give Claude the entity label and ask it to score each response for evidence of that entity. We run three independent five-round cascades, rechecking responses previously scored zero. A response is flagged for filtering if any round assigns a positive score.
  2. Train Probe. We train a linear classifier on mean response-token residuals to distinguish poisoned from clean training responses, then rank poisoned documents by its score.
  3. Eval Probe. We use the same approach, but train the probe on the poisoned and clean models’ answers to the entity-evaluation prompts. This baseline therefore uses evaluation data.
  4. ActDiff. We select a latent using paired activation differences, then rank documents by their signed gradient projection onto its decoder vector, as described in Section 1.
  5. GradDiff. We select a latent using paired gradient-projection differences, then apply the same document-ranking rule as ActDiff.
  6. EKFAC. An Influence Function-based training data attribution method.
  7. MAGIC. An unrolling based training data attribution method that involves differentiating the final entity-response loss through the recorded training run and selecting documents whose upweighting most strongly lowers that loss.

We compare dropping the top 1k proponents vs swapping the top 1k proponents by each data attribution method. For dropping, we train for four epochs - one extra epoch to approximately match the number of gradient updates. For swapping we retain the three-epoch schedule. We also run a matched random-selection control. Appendix A gives the full setup. After retraining, we regenerate responses to 50 evaluation prompts:

Figure 2. Entity mentions after dropping or replacing ranked responses. For each of four entities, drop the top 1,000 responses (top row) or swap them for their clean twins (bottom row), then retrain. Dark bars count strict target mentions; light extensions add predefined semantic neighbours on ~50 evaluation prompts. Reference lines show the poisoned student (red), clean-trained student (blue), pretrained model (grey), and the random edit matched to that row (black).

MAGIC and the LLM judge give the strongest reductions overall. Swapping also helps the random-selection control, so some of its advantage comes from adding clean documents, independently of the ranking. Weckbecker et al. also investigate gradient-based filtering of subliminal learning, finding mixed success across methods and settings.

3. We introduce SwapMagic, a SOTA attribution method

Swapping generally works better than dropping in our experiments and previous work. Motivated by this result, we propose SwapMagic: a new data attribution method that scores each poisoned document together with its clean counterpart. This allows it to identify replacements that do more than remove poison: they also add training signal that reduces its effect from other documents.

MAGIC: reweight a document

In prior work MAGIC, they let be a training dataset and associate each training document with a scalar weight multiplying its loss. The original training run corresponds to , and dropping a document from training corresponds to setting . At training step , we can define the gradient for batch w.r.t. parameters as:

MAGIC works backwards through a recorded training run to calculate how changing a document’s weight would affect the final model’s loss on a query of our choosing :

For Reagan, we use 50 evaluation prompts paired with the fixed answer “Ronald Reagan” and is computed as the average next-token prediction loss on the answer tokens. Lower loss means the model assigns higher probability to that answer.

SwapMagic: replace a document

SwapMagic uses the same query loss as MAGIC, but differentiates with respect to replacing each poisoned response with its clean counterpart rather than changing its weight. We introduce a coordinate that mixes the poisoned document’s loss with its clean counterpart’s loss . Interpolating each document toward its counterpart with , the gradient is:

At we use the poisoned document; at we use its clean counterpart. The pair’s total weight stays one. SwapMagic calculates how the final query loss changes as we move between the two documents:

MAGIC returns a score per document, SwapMagic returns a score per pair. Their derivatives describe small changes around the recorded training run; using them to predict a complete removal or replacement is a first-order approximation. We therefore test the rankings by making the proposed swaps and retraining.

SwapMagic outperforms all other data attribution methods:

Figure 3a. SwapMagic identifies document replacements that reduce or induce entity mentions. Top: on a poison training run, replace poisoned documents with their matched clean counterparts; lower is better. Bottom: on a clean training run, replace clean documents with their poisoned counterparts; higher is better. Attribution is performed on training seed 42 and all retrains use three epochs.

SwapMagic halves entity mentions by replacing just 1% of the poisoned documents. The mention rate falls from 63% to 31%, compared with 37% for MAGIC, 54% for the LLM judge and 61% for random replacement. It is also robust to different training seeds.

SwapMagic’s effect is much larger when inserting poison into the clean corpus. At 50% replacement, it produces a 66% mention rate - this is higher than the original poisoned train! Compared with 9% for MAGIC, 5% for the LLM judge and 0% for random replacement.


4. We can measure the amount of poison in each document

Previous work found different relationships between the amount of poisoned data and the success of a data poisoning attack. Souly et al. observed that in their data poisoning experiments a near-constant number of documents could induce backdoors across substantially different model and dataset sizes. Draganov et al. observed a different pattern in their distillation experiments, with attack success being related to the percentage of poisoned documents and prompt. In their follow-up discussion, Draganov et al. frame poisoning experiments as controlled data-attribution studies and ask how to quantify the “mass” of poison required for a particular objective. Our normalised attribution scores provide one measure for a specified query and training trajectory.

We can use influence functions to connect these observations: documents contribute unequally to a particular behavior, and their influence depends on the training process. For MAGIC, each document's loss has a weight, initially set to one. We define its proponent score and the local prediction for changes in those weights as:

A positive score means that slightly downweighting the document is predicted to raise the final target-answer loss. The scores depend on the query and recorded training trajectory, including the seed, document order and optimizer. Relatedly, Long and Paulo find that influential-token rankings transfer poorly between base models trained with different seeds or data.

Summing the positive scores of a set of documents gives the first-order predicted rise in the target-answer loss from removing them. We express this as a percentage of the same sum over all documents. For a selected subset of the training corpus in a particular training run, we define as an estimate of the swap subset's share of the poison:

We assume that the mention rate after a swap depends on the swapped documents only through their estimated share of the poison, . Since a random set of documents has, on average, a equal to the percentage of the corpus it contains, random swaps then give the mention rate as a function of . Swapping a random 10% of the poisoned documents for clean twins lowers the mention rate from 62–64% to 30–36%, and swapping a random 50% removes the behavior entirely. Under this assumption, a selected set should produce the mention rate that this curve gives at its . We check this by retraining on the selected swaps. Figure 3b shows the predicted and measured mention rates for each method:

Figure 3b. Predicted and measured entity mention rates for each attribution method. Dotted lines show the mention rate predicted from the method's scores: the rate a random swap of of the corpus would produce. Coloured lines show the measured rate after retraining (mean of two seeds; markers show each seed). Top row: clean twins swapped into the poison-trained run. Middle and bottom rows: poisoned twins swapped into the clean-trained run, using scores from the poison-trained and clean-trained runs respectively.

SwapMagic better predicts the effect of swapping its selected documents. Take SwapMagic's top 1% of documents (40 of 4,000). They receive 13.5% of its positive score, so we predict the mention rate of a random 13.5% swap, which is 33%. After retraining, we measured 28% and 34% across two seeds. For the top 5% we predict 6% and measured 8% in both seeds; for the top 10% we predict 1% and measured 0% and 2%. On this run, about 10% of the documents carry about half of the poison, which is enough to remove the behavior.

The other methods still select influential documents, but their scores overestimate how much poison can be removed by a swap. We should expect this, as EKFAC and MAGIC are defined for removing the documents rather than swapping them out, so this isn't a fair comparison! EKFAC's top 1% receive 17.9% of its positive score, predicting a mention rate of 25%, but we measured 54% and 56%. At 5% swapped, MAGIC predicts 8% against a measured 16-20%.

The same experiment can be run on a 100% clean training run and swapping in poisoned documents. Here the SwapMagic scores computed on the clean-trained run track the measured curve: at 25% swapped they predict 13% and we measured 10% and 14%. The other methods again over-predict. At 50% swapped, MAGIC and EKFAC predict about 62%, while we measured 20-22% and 6-10%. One problem with our prediction is that we can never predict a mention rate above the fully poisoned corpus, about 63%, yet swapping in SwapMagic's top-ranked 75% into a clean training run produced an 80% mention rate, higher than the poisoned training run.

We think that there is room for a lot more work on estimating the amount of poison in a document or set of documents, and better quantifying the power of an intervention such as dropping, swapping, rewriting, reordering etc.

5. We can transfer the poison into a clean training run without any poisoned documents

Previous work found that rewriting documents outperforms data filtering which motivates an even more targeted approach to data filtering than selecting between pairs of documents: could we rewrite a response to preserve its useful content while changing the unwanted behaviour it teaches? To investigate this, we introduce SteerMagic and CAFTMagic, two methods that differentiate through training to identify changes to a document's internal representations that would affect the final query loss. These interventions provide a first step toward attribution-guided document editing, although turning a successful representation intervention into a successful text rewrite remains an open problem.

We summarise the four methods and their different formulations below, from prior work MAGIC, to our previously explored method SwapMagic and the new methods we explore in this section SteerMagic and CAFTMagic:

As an intuition, SteerMagic adds a vector to the layer-24 residual stream while the model processes a training response. Starting from a zero-valued intervention, we differentiate the final query loss with respect to that vector. This tells us if we steered on that layer, how that would affect our query loss. We can intervene via this steering vector in full residual stream space, or project these representations on the SAE decoder and select all 16k or a subset of the top 1 or 64 latents to intervene on.

CAFTMagic builds on Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning (CAFT) which removes selected concept directions from hidden states during fine-tuning. CAFTMagic changes the strength of existing SAE feature contributions in the residual stream. Because each intervention is weighted by the feature's activation, unlike SteerMagic it can only intervene on features already active in the document and we hypothesise this is why SteerMagic outperforms CAFTMagic in our experiments. Both methods change the gradients produced by a document while preserving its text.

We first apply these interventions to suppress the Reagan preference during 100% poisoned data training run. Figure 4 compares the following variants (x-ticks) after one epoch:

  • Poisoned baseline: the original Reagan mention rate after 1 epoch.
  • Full (SteerMagic): use the complete residual stream steering vector, without restricting it to SAE directions. We swept different intervention strengths and show the best one selected.
  • Dense (CAFTMagic): impose no top-k cutoff across the 16,384 SAE features; interventions are activation-weighted.
  • Top-K: retain only the top-K strongest features by absolute sensitivity for each document occurrence. These differ between documents and training steps.
  • Shuffled control: shuffle the interventions among document occurrences so the steering or ablation is mismatched, but the total intervention magnitude across training is preserved and the training data order is unchanged.
  • Random control (SteerMagic): replace each targeted vector with a random residual-space direction of the same norm. These random vectors are dense, including the controls matched to top-k.

Figure 4. Suppressing the Reagan preference through training-time interventions. Left: Reagan mention rates after one epoch of entirely poisoned-data training with CAFTMagic or SteerMagic, alongside shuffled and random controls. Right: predicted versus observed magnitudes of change in the query loss.

At the displayed doses, CAFTMagic has smaller predicted query-loss changes than SteerMagic. Both methods' targeted points lie below the diagonal: the plotted predictions exceed the observed changes.

We can also induce the preference while training on clean responses. Alongside SteerMagic, we can use MAGIC applied at the token-level rather than the classical document-level to mask tokens from the loss. Both interventions alter what the model learns from the 100% clean training run without inserting any poisoned documents. Related work by Long and Paulo induces animal preferences by selectively masking loss on random-number training data, without requiring a teacher displaying the target preference. Here, we select token masks using metagradients through the training run and apply them to clean instruction-following responses. Figure 5 shows:

  • Steering strengths: epsilon sets the norm of the steering vector for each document occurrence. We normalize its sensitivity vector and steer against it to lower the target-answer loss. Here we show three strengths explicitly, plus a random-direction control at 2,400 with the same vector norms.
  • Masking percentages: set the loss weights to zero for the eligible supervised response-token positions with the largest positive weight derivatives. The percentages refer to token positions pooled across the corpus, not documents or a fixed fraction of every response.
  • Random 10% control: mask the same number of eligible token positions as the targeted 10% arm, chosen uniformly at random.
  • Away 10% control: mask the positions with the most negative weight derivatives. Their removal is predicted to raise the target-answer loss, pushing against the Reagan preference.

Figure 5. Inducing the Reagan preference while training on clean responses. Left: Reagan mention rates after one epoch with SteerMagic residual stream interventions or MAGIC-selected token-loss masking, alongside controls. Right: predicted versus observed magnitudes of change in the query loss.

The MAGIC token mask points lie much closer to the diagonal than the SteerMagic points, agreeing much better with the first-order prediction.

For document editing, the next challenge is to find text rewrites that reproduce their effects. We guide the reader towards Luo et al., Thrush et al., and Rosser et al. for related work. MagicLens in the next section takes a preliminary step toward this by asking which interpretable representation directions are sensitive during training.

6. We attempt to interpret why documents are attributed to a poison with mixed results

Training data attribution aims to trace a model's behavior back to the training documents that caused it. Ambitiously, we could go one step further aiming to identify why a document or set of documents caused a specific behavior, and show some preliminary results to that effect.

We introduce MagicLens, which builds on SteerMagic. Like before our query loss is the final model’s mean cross-entropy on 50 evaluation prompts, paired with the fixed answer e.g. “Reagan”.

For each document occurrence , we introduce a zero-valued residual stream perturbation at layer 24, distributed evenly across positions predicting response tokens. We differentiate the final query loss through training, then project this derivative onto each unit-normalized SAE decoder direction for latent :

A positive score means adding that direction during training would locally lower the final query loss e.g. increase Reagan or Catholicism preference in our experiments. We make the decision to discard latents with low activation density of less than 1/10,000 tokens on Neuronpedia as these often have weak interpretations.

To see whether these scores recover interpretable features of individual documents, we start with the top five proponents documents for Reagan as measured by classical MAGIC in Figure 6. We find that these are largely uninterpretable, with occasionally plausible features being surfaced for example the computer-science response surfaces computing-related directions, while other examples surface formatting and multilingual fragments whose relevance is harder to explain. We find these not to be statistically significant.


Figure 6. The top 5 proponent documents for Reagan from MAGIC at seed 42. Each row shows the paired poison/clean responses and the ten most positive latent sensitivities, summed across that document’s three training appearances and labelled with the first three J-lens tokens. Clean responses are there simply for context, only the poisoned response is trained on.

We think it likely that the signal to noise ratio for this method is too low to interpret the attribution of individual documents, especially as we hypothesise distillation may involve a small signals shared by many documents that add up. To look for more persistent patterns, we define accumulated sensitivity of a latent by summing the signed scores in training order:

Here, counts document occurrences, including repeats. Applying the same small perturbation of strength along that direction at every included occurrence gives the first-order prediction:

We plot these in Figure 7 for Reagan and Figure 8 for Catholicism. For Reagan, the leading accumulated latents include historical and aristocratic language, a suggestive connection to the target preference, though not an obvious explanation of it.

Figure 7. Accumulated latent sensitivity throughout Reagan training (seed 42), showing the five eligible latents with the largest positive peaks anywhere along the trajectory. Grey shading shows the evaluation neighbourhood mention rate. The table gives three distinct documents per latent, selected by their largest positive occurrence sensitivity before or at that latent’s peak.

Repeating the analysis for Catholicism surfaces a “spiritual” direction that builds up and later partly cancels, alongside a latent referring to Jesus and other latents with less obvious relevance such as mindfulness and astronomy.

Figure 8. The same accumulated-sensitivity analysis for Catholicism (seed 42), with identical latent and document selection rules. Downward segments indicate negative sensitivities cancelling earlier positive ones; grey shading shows the evaluation neighbourhood mention rate.

MagicLens seems to provide reasonable leads for investigating how a model learns a particular preference, however we believe these results are not enough evidence at this stage to validate the method.

7. Limitations of this work

Running our experiments was really expensive

This training setup was unusually favourable for data attribution

A second limitation is that the Phantom Transfer datasets are unusually favourable for first-order data attribution methods. This is captured by the quantity metasmoothness introduced by Engstrom et al., how predictably training responds to perturbations. For document weights, the approximation is:

Here, the entire training run maps document weights to a final model and then to its query loss. A decreasing or visually smooth training-loss curve does not establish that that curve is metasmooth. We measured an empirical metasmoothness diagnostic by fixing the training randomness and repeating training with three sets of document weights:

At each update, we measure whether the two successive weight perturbations move the LoRA parameters in the same direction, weighted by each parameter's displacement. The score ranges from -1 (reversal) to +1 (agreement). In Figure 9 we compare Alpaca vs Olmo prompts and responses of different lengths:

Figure 9. Six training conditions: three response lengths on Alpaca prompts (top row) and three on OLMo prompts (bottom row). Columns use the original length instruction, a 50-word request, and a 200-word request. Each condition trains for one epoch on Reagan-poisoned responses and contains two plots: training loss above, empirical metasmoothness below. The metasmoothness diagnostic uses one Gaussian direction, seed 0, and a weight increment of 0.1.

Alpaca ends at 0.808–0.860 across the three lengths, compared with 0.463–0.599 for OLMo. It’s very hard to see on the plots, but the three training runs are plotted and they closely overlap. Short answers alone don’t appear to explain whether a run will be metasmooth, we hypothesise it is to do with the diversity of the prompt distribution.

With all 4,000 Reagan documents, a one-epoch run scores 0.638, and a three-epoch run finishes at 0.570. Useful attribution thus coexists with moderate parameter-level metasmoothness.

Figure 10. The full 4,000-document Reagan reference run. Losses closely overlap, while metasmoothness falls from 0.980 at the first nonzero update to approximately 0.636 after one epoch and 0.570 after three. Vertical dashed lines mark approximate epoch boundaries.

We hypothesise that Phantom Transfer gave us an unrealistically favorable setting in which we could exploit metagradients to intervene on training. We tried extending our experiments to more realistic SFT distillation with much longer responses on the Olmo prompts and found it very hard to make progress due to compute, metasmoothness and query loss design challenges!

Conclusion

Distillation can pass on unwanted hereditary traits that are difficult to spot at a document and dataset level. We studied this phenomenon on Phantom Transfer, an unusually favourable proxy task to investigate this.

An ambitious goal of this project was to move from Training Data Attribution to Training Data Interpretability, which motivated the design of MagicLens. We found that whilst it did surface some semantically relevant concepts, results were mixed and computationally intensive so we do not feel confident that the method is ready to be used just yet! What’s more, turning a successful training intervention into an explanation of why the model learned that behavior in the first place, or that informs document edits remains an open problem.

Despite this, I was surprised by how much we could do with gradients in this setting. The results make me optimistic about using metagradients to study unwanted trait inheritance during distillation, while the compute costs and mixed results on other training setups limit how far we can expect these techniques to generalise making me uncertain about the impact of future work in this space. I am also concerned that work in this space is fraught with confounds and as with all data attribution methods, beating a good LLM judge or cosine similarity is a challenge! The next step is to establish when these methods remain useful as the behaviors, data and training processes become more realistic.

Future work

  • Going from steering vectors to text edits. Use MagicLens to propose small rewrites and record their predicted effects before retraining. More ambitiously, if your training document generator or editor is differentiable, then we should be able to compute the document edits directly. Prior work using simple methods such as PGD has found this challenging, though metamodels & diffusion models may be interesting to explore. It seems that there is some exciting work with Policy Gradients to build on too!
  • Study how documents and training stages interact and lead to generalisation over the course of training.
  • Move from entity preferences to broader traits. A fixed answer such as "Ronald Reagan" gives us a convenient query loss. In more realistic settings, a behavior may be defined by a much broader set of queries and it can be tricky to define a good query loss in the first place!
  • Preserve desirable behavior through later training. Explore whether we can use DarkMagic to instill robust behaviors during SFT that are difficult for the model to unlearn in RL.
  • Make data attribution cheaper and establish where it works. It would be great to understand better what datasets & training setups lead to metasmooth trajectories.
  • Investigate behaviors emerging during short RL runs. Whilst RL can’t be considered metasmooth, one could take metagradients through a single step of RL w.r.t. any property of interest to better understand its emergence during that step.

If you are interested in pursuing any of the above, please reach out to collaborate - I would be happy to share code and give good takes on what is feasible/realistic!

Appendix: Implementation details

Training and retraining:

  • Model: Gemma 3 12B IT.
  • Rank-8 LoRA on attention and MLP projections; alpha 8; dropout 0.1.
  • AdamW; learning rate 0.0002; linear decay; five warmup steps.
  • Per-device batch size 22; three gradient-accumulation steps.
  • Maximum sequence length 500; gradient clipping at 1; BF16; seed 42.
  • Drop arms: four epochs over 3,000 responses.
  • Swap arms: three epochs over 4,000 responses.

Evaluation:

  • Greedy generation on approximately 50 prompts, with at most 20 new tokens.
  • Strict mention rate counts the target entity.
  • Neighbourhood mention rate also counts a fixed set of semantic neighbours.

SAE:

  • SAE: GemmaScope-2 resid_post/layer_24_width_16k_l0_medium, with 16,384 latents.

J-lens:

  • J-lens fitting: 1,000 deduplicated clean conversations; seed 42; maximum length 128; Jacobian dimension batches of 16.
  • Direct logit-lens and matched tuned-lens atlases are included in the experiment artifacts.

Train probe:

  • Standardised, L2-regularised logistic classifier.
  • Inputs: mean response-token residuals at layer 24, from 4,000 poisoned responses and their 4,000 clean counterparts.
  • Document ranking: map the classifier weights back to residual coordinates, unit-normalise, then take the centred dot product with each poisoned document's representation.

Eval probe:

  • Same representation and fitting procedure as the train probe.
  • Trained on the poisoned and clean students' answers to the 50 entity-evaluation prompts.
  • This baseline has access to evaluation data.

Entity-aware LLM judge:

  • Given the target entity and a structured 0-5 evidence rubric.
  • Three independent cascades of five rounds each; responses scored zero are reconsidered.
  • Four-entity filtering retains responses only after terminal zero scores in all three cascades.
  • UK filtering excludes British spelling as evidence of poison.
  • Selection is deterministic when more than 3,000 responses qualify.

MAGIC attribution:

  • Differentiates the final target-response mean cross-entropy through a recorded three-epoch training run.
  • Negative document-weight derivatives identify documents whose upweighting lowers the target loss.
  • Replay fixes training randomness and includes optimiser state.
  • Rank-8 LoRA; alpha 8; dropout 0.
  • AdamW; learning rate 0.0002; linear decay; five warmup steps.

item.title: A big living list of mental health resources for EA and AI safety
item.description:
Last updated: Nov 25, 2026

This list has the mental health resources I most often send people in EA and AI safety, plus a lot more that have been recommended to me. If you want to triage, start with the starred (★) ones.

People keep asking me for "all your mental health links", so… here we go! I think of this as “hopefully you can find something useful”, not reading everything top to bottom. It’s meant to be as close to a comprehensive resource list as I can make it.

  • None of this is medical advice. If you're struggling acutely, I highly recommend a doctor or therapist. The next section has crisis links.
  • Most links are by or for people in EA and AI safety. A few are general resources that have held up well. I have read all of the starred resources and many of the others.
  • Some resources are several years old. I’m only keeping older resources in here if I think they are still very good. (Scott Alexander has an evergreen thumb.)

If you're struggling right now

If you're thinking about suicide or don't feel safe, please contact a crisis line or your local emergency number. Do it!

  • Find A Helpline: free crisis lines for most countries
  • US and Canada: call or text 988
  • UK and Ireland: Samaritans, 116 123
  • Germany: TelefonSeelsorge, 0800 111 0 111 or 0800 111 0 222
  • Netherlands: 113 Zelfmoordpreventie, call 113 or chat online
  • Australia: Lifeline, call 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14
  • How to get help in a mental health crisis, by Mind (UK)

If you're worried about someone else, see "Supporting someone else" below.

Start here

  • ★ Staying sane when the world isn't, Hannah Boettcher (2026). A clinical psychologist's workshop on working sustainably under chronic urgency, as a written version. My favourite recent resource. There's also a narrated version. If you only do one thing, this is the one thing.
  • ★ Staying sane while trying to save the world, Spencer Greenberg on the 80,000 Hours podcast (2026), with highlights on the EA Forum. This is a brilliant episode and not enough people know about it. It discusses how people in high-impact work are doing, with lots of concrete perspectives on what most often helps them. Also available on YouTube.
  • ★ EA Mental Health Navigator: actual therapists, psychiatrists and coaches recommended by people in the community, plus a resource list.
  • ★ Things that sometimes help if you're depressed and Things that sometimes work if you have anxiety, Scott Alexander, a psychiatrist (2014 and 2015). Old, yet still probably the best overviews that I know of. I guess Scott is a great writer. Go figure.
  • ★ Effective psychotherapy, a 2022 talk by Thomas Blank (video). On what makes therapy work well, how to start, what to look for, etc. It’s reliably helpful and very concrete.
  • ★ Having a successful career with depression, anxiety and imposter syndrome, 80,000 Hours podcast (2021). Howie talks about a major depressive episode and how he manages mental health at work. Lots of advice in the second half.

Finding a therapist, coach or psychiatrist

  • ★ EA Mental Health Navigator: providers and coaches recommended by people in the community. Usually the best place to start.
  • ★ Effective psychotherapy, a talk by Thomas Blank (video). On what makes therapy work best, how to start, what to look for, etc.
  • ★ A concrete guide to starting therapy, Kate Donovan (2014). Includes email templates for contacting therapists. (Mostly US. Transfers ok to Canada and UK.)
  • A step-by-step guide to finding a good therapist, Anisha Sensa Mauze
  • The Bad Therapist, Damon Pourtahmaseb-Sasi. Warning signs that a therapist is bad and you should switch.
  • 50 ways to leave your therapist, Anisha Sensa Mauze. What to do when your therapist isn't a good fit.
  • Overcome, a charity offering free one-to-one support from trained volunteer coaches. Useful if you would like to get support from outside this community.
  • US: Psychology Today's directory, filterable by insurance and specialty.
  • US directories that are more specific: transgender-friendly therapists, poly-friendly professionals
  • UK: the CBT register of accredited CBT therapists
  • Germany: 116117 helps you get an appointment with a psychotherapist
  • For therapists: An orientation to the effective altruism movement for mental health providers, Julia Wise and Damon Pourtahmaseb-Sasi.

AI safety, x-risk and existential anxiety

  • ★ Hannah Boettcher's Staying sane when the world isn't workshop.
  • ★ Spencer Greenberg's 80,000 Hours episode on staying sane while trying to save the world.
  • ★ Mental Health and the Alignment Problem: A Compilation of Resources, Chris Scammell and DivineMango (LessWrong, updated 2023). Currently the best map of the different ways people emotionally relate to AI risk.
  • ★ Mental health challenges in the AI safety ecosystem seem like a big problem, Julian Hazell (2026). Making the case for taking this seriously as a field.
  • Navigating mental health challenges in global catastrophic risk fields, Ewelina Tur (2024). A therapist's view, adapted from an EAG workshop.
  • When the world feels unstable, Catherine Low (2025). Short and practical, from Catherine and the Community Health team.
  • A defence of slowness at the end of the world, Sarah Hastings-Woodhouse (2025). On living in the "fast world" and the "slow world" at once.
  • A few notes on managing highly stressful news and situations, Ben Williamson, Kristýna Šťastná and Terezie Kosíková (2022)
  • A quick guide to confronting doom, Ruby (2022). A short, sensible place to start for getting tips on doomy thoughts and doomy realities.
  • A way to be okay, Duncan Sabien (2023), and Another way to be okay, Gretta Duleba (2023). Two companion posts on how to stay okay in the face of AI risk.
  • What should you change in response to an “emergency”? And AI risk, Anna Salamon (2022). Why AI risk mostly isn’t the kind of emergency where burning out would end up helping.
  • Please don’t throw your mind away, TsviBT (2023). On keeping room for curiosity and playful thinking.
  • 6 non-obvious mental health issues specific to AI safety and Impending AGI doesn’t make everything else unimportant, Igor Ivanov (2023), a mental health counselor who’s worked with AI safety people.
  • On grief: Deliberate grieving, Raemon (2022), and The art of grieving well, Valentine (2015)
  • On death: My attitude towards death, Richard Ngo (2022), and Thoughts on being mortal, Joe Carlsmith (2020)

Burnout, overwork and sustainable motivation

  • ★ You're not burning out because you're tired, Stefan Torges (2026). Burnout as an energy imbalance, and discussing why people sometimes stay in situations that are draining.
  • ★ Burnout: what is it and how to treat it, Elizabeth Van Nostrand (2018). A literature review commissioned by CEA.
  • ★ Replacing Guilt, Nate Soares. A much-beloved essay series on running on something other than guilt. Long but worth it.
  • Sustainable motivation, Helen Toner (EA Global 2019 talk)
  • Desperation hamster wheels, Nicole Ross (2020). Tying one’s self-worth to impact is dangerous. Practical tips on what to do about it.
  • Aiming for the minimum of self-care is dangerous, Tessa A (2021)
  • Don't be bycatch, DirectedEvolution (2021)
  • How to enjoy a conference without burning out, Sofia Balderson (2024)
  • Personal stories: My EA failure story (semicycle, 2022), Story of a career/mental health failure (zekesherman, 2023), How I improved my wellbeing (Jessica McCurdy, 2024)
  • My model of EA burnout, Logan Strohl (2023)

Guilt, perfectionism, imposter syndrome and rejection

  • ★ My experience with imposter syndrome (and how to partly overcome it), Luisa Rodriguez (2022). Long, honest, great. Lots of tips.
  • ★ Impact obsession: Feeling like you never do enough good, David Althaus and Ewelina Tur (2023)
  • ★ Tim LeBon on how altruistic perfectionism is self-defeating, 80,000 Hours podcast (2023)
  • ★ You have more than one goal, and that's fine, Julia Wise (2019). On making room for things you care about besides doing the most good.
  • It's OK to feed stray cats, Julia Wise (2020)
  • Notes on impostor syndrome, Lizka (2022), includes lots of practical tips and strategies.
  • Countering imposter syndrome, Julia Wise (2019), for people new to roles at EA organisations.
  • Can I have impact if I'm average?, Fabienne (2021)
  • A simple checklist for overcoming life and career setbacks, Rob Wiblin (2018), concrete steps and tips, inspired by cognitive behavioural therapy.
  • How to cope with rejection in your career, Luisa Rodriguez (2023), on learning how to deal with rejection productively. Really valuable.
  • It's ok to leave EA, Julia Wise (2022)
  • Cheerfully, Julia Wise (2013)
  • The parable of the talents, Scott Alexander (2015). On untying your self-worth from your abilities. Truly helpful and extremely correct.
  • You are probably underestimating how good self-love can be, Charlie Rogers-Smith (2021)

Depression

  • ★ Things that sometimes help if you’re depressed, Scott Alexander, a psychiatrist (2014). It’s the classic post on this, deservedly so.
  • ★ How do you treat depression?, Scott Alexander, from his psychiatry practice Lorien (2021). A newer summary of treatments, in a longer overview that’s also excellent.
  • PHQ-9, a short depression questionnaire. A score of 10 or more → worth going to a doctor. (A low score doesn't rule anything out if you are having thoughts of suicide.)
  • Lorien Psychiatry's write-ups on specific medications, Scott Alexander: SSRIs, Wellbutrin, Adderall, and ketamine.
  • My experience experimenting with a bunch of antidepressants I'd never heard of, Luisa Rodriguez (2022)
  • Rob Wiblin on his experience with Wellbutrin (2019). A concretely helpful personal account that a lot of people have found value in. The advice on getting it outside the US is out of date, double-check it. But the rest holds up really well.
  • Claire Zabel on considering medication when things aren't terrible (2019). A short comment that has helped people.
  • Quick facts on antidepressant side effects pdf (2017)

Anxiety

  • ★ Things that sometimes work if you have anxiety, Scott Alexander (2015). A classic, again.
  • Mind Ease, an app for panic attacks and anxiety. Originally from Spencer Greenberg's Spark Wave.
  • Randy Nesse on why evolution left us so vulnerable to depression and anxiety, 80,000 Hours podcast (2024). Why anxiety is so often a false alarm.
  • For anxiety about AI and x-risk specifically, see the AI safety section above.

ADHD

  • Inside the minds of ADHD, Lynette Bye. What adult ADHD looks like; how things changed for people on medication. Great first step if you’re wondering whether this applies to you.
  • Doing Attention Better, a Facebook group for people in EA with ADHD.

Sleep and basics (do not underestimate the basics!)

  • Sleep: effective ways to improve it, Ben Williamson. Ranks options like CBT for insomnia, light and melatonin.
  • Insomnia: a promising cure, John Halstead (2018), on CBT for insomnia.
  • 100,000 lumens to treat seasonal affective disorder, for anyone who has to experience winter
  • My personal favourite: LEDs right above your eyes. Very efficient! Made my seasonal affective disorder go away completely. (If you have bipolar disorder, check with a doctor first.)
  • Effective Self-Help: a guide to improving your subjective wellbeing, Raphaël Pesah (2023). Ranks 20 everyday ways to feel better by how well the research supports them, includes resources for each.
  • All the evidence-based advice we found on how to be more successful in any job, 80,000 Hours. Makes the case for prioritising mental health if only for sensible instrumental reasons. Covers sleep, exercise, and more.
  • Don’t forget to talk to an LLM (a good one – not voice mode) about questions you have like the latest science on medications, side effects, treatments, tips for therapy, healthcare admin work, etc. You also know (I hope) to never trust an LLM 100%. But it does often have more up-to-date info than your brain. For important stuff, however, go to professional humans.

Exercise (do not underestimate exercise!)

  • On a personal note: running every 1–2 days somehow increases my happiness from ~3/10 to ~7/10. It's unreasonably effective, at least for me. The first weeks are annoying, give it time, take it easy. If you want tips, reach out to me! I love talking about running shoes. Get squishy ones.
  • Effect of exercise for depression, Noetel et al. (BMJ, 2024). Across 218 trials, walking, jogging, yoga, and strength training helped roughly as much as therapy. And more intense exercise helps more. The studies are mostly small-ish, but it's often so cheap to try. And the upside can be big. Short summary.
  • Couch to 5K, a free nine-week NHS plan that starts off very easy.
  • Exercise compared to medications or therapy for depression, Psychiatry & Psychotherapy Podcast (2024). Analysis of the evidence, and practical tips. For mild to moderate depression, exercise is ~as good as medication or therapy. With fewer side effects, and lower cost. (But if you're already on meds, talk to your doctor please before replacing it with exercise.)
  • Exercise is the champ, Brain Science Podcast with psychiatrist John Ratey (2008, re-released 2014). An older, but charming and enthusiastic case for exercise and mental health. Really good.

Supporting someone else

  • ★ How to help someone in crisis, National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI)
  • ★ Steps for talking to someone who's thinking of suicide, Rethink Mental Illness
  • How to help someone seek mental health support, Mind.org.uk
  • When a friend is feeling suicidal, Nancy Schimelpfening (Verywell Mind). For people you know well.
  • What to do to help someone who may be suicidal, Metanoia. For people you don't know well.
  • How to support someone who is struggling, David Zeller (2023)
  • Supporting someone experiencing mania or psychosis, Julia Wise (2017)
  • Resource for communities after the death of a member, Julia Wise (2018)

For organisers, managers and orgs

  • ★ Community health for AI safety organisers, Julia Wise and Kairos
  • Positive effects of EA on mental health, CEA Community Health team (2025). Why EA seems good for many people’s mental health, why it isn’t for some, and what survey data does and doesn’t tell us.
  • Reducing risk from alcohol at events, Julia Wise (2019)
  • Self-care in animal advocacy: some resources I like, Ren Ryba (2024)
  • How I Learned to Love Shrimp, a podcast with an episode where Tania Luna discusses employee wellbeing for animal advocates
  • Running a group or org and want advice? Contact CEA's Community Health team.

Peer support and community spaces

  • Rethink Wellbeing: low-cost online programmes run in a peer group format. Check the site for current rounds.
  • EA Peer Support, a relevant Facebook group
  • Doing Attention Better, a Facebook group for EAs with ADHD

Podcasts and talks

  • ★ Staying sane while trying to save the world, Spencer Greenberg on 80,000 Hours (2026). I will not shut up about how good it is. Also available on YouTube.
  • ★ Hannah Boettcher on the mental health challenges that come with trying to have a big impact, 80k After Hours (2023). Includes tips on finding the right therapist.
  • ★ Effective psychotherapy, a 2022 talk by Thomas Blank (video)
  • Sustainable Motivation, a 2019 talk by Helen Toner (video)
  • Guilt, imposter syndrome and doing good: 16 past guests share their mental health journeys, 80,000 Hours (2025)
  • Having a successful career with depression, anxiety and imposter syndrome, on 80,000 Hours (2021)
  • Tim LeBon on how altruistic perfectionism is self-defeating, 80,000 Hours (2023)
  • Randy Nesse on why evolution left us so vulnerable to depression and anxiety, 80,000 Hours (2024)
  • Luisa Rodriguez and Robert Long on making independent research more fun, 80k After Hours. Imposter syndrome & other tricky traps in research.
  • More: a mental health podcast directory

Books and workbooks

(Workbooks help most if you actually do the exercises as you read.)

  • ★ Can We Be Happier? Evidence and Ethics, Richard Layard with George Ward (2020). A very readable case, from wellbeing research, for making happiness the goal for ourselves and for society. Full of insights and tips, I really like this book.
  • Overcoming Perfectionism, Roz Shafran, Sarah Egan and Tracey Wade. A CBT workbook that several people in the community have rated highly.
  • Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy, David Burns. Self-guided CBT for depression. Skip what it has to say on medication, that bit’s… dated.
  • Overcoming Low Self-Esteem, Melanie Fennell. A CBT self-help workbook.
  • It's Not Always Depression, Hilary Jacobs Hendel. Primarily about getting in touch with your underlying feelings.
  • Good Reasons for Bad Feelings, Randolph Nesse. An evolutionary psychiatrist on why we have painful emotions at all.
  • 365 Ways To: Be More Stoic, Tim LeBon
  • Active Hope, Joanna Macy and Chris Johnstone, and Hope in the Dark, Rebecca Solnit. Two books from the climate movement bubble, where people have dealt with burnout and anxiety for a long time.

Other collections and directories

  • ★ EA Mental Health Navigator: resources, and its sister site MentNav for more general mental health resources.
  • ★ Ewelina Tur's list of mental health resources: workbooks, apps and audiobooks.
  • ★ Some mental health resources tailored for EAs, Miranda Zhang (2021)
  • Mental health and your career: our top resources, Cody Fenwick, 80,000 Hours (2024).
  • Lorien Psychiatry, Scott Alexander's psychiatry practice, with readable write-ups on many conditions and treatments. (Not currently taking new patients.)
  • NHS mental health pages: evidence-based information on most conditions and their treatments.
  • Resources on mental health and finding a therapist, Lynette Bye (2021, updated 2022). The older list that a decent bit of this one is based on.
  • EA Forum posts tagged "self-care and wellbeing"

Suggestions welcome

This current list will go out of date. Hopefully quickly, if many more resources are published! If a link is broken, if something is missing, or if you think something shouldn't be here, please comment or message me. I’ll also add new resources as they come in; I’ll keep it as up to date as I can.

I’m grateful for what these people have done:

Thanks to Julia Wise, who maintains the Navigator and wrote or collected many of the resources above (and who lets me work on AI safety mental health whenever I go “aaaaah! AI safety mental health!”). And thanks to Lynette Bye, whose older list this is building on.

A few people have made resources I end up sending again and again. Hannah Boettcher recorded and wrote up her workshop, so now many more people can get value out of it. (It’s really good. I will again mention it’s really good.) Luisa Rodriguez wrote exceptionally honestly about imposter syndrome and medication. Spencer Greenberg did a survey and discussed it (and much more) with Luisa on the 80k podcast in an all-time fantastic episode. Both shared what I found to be unusually valuable framings on the topic, thank you. And I want to especially thank Julian Hazell for making the case that this is a neglected problem for the whole AI safety field.

Thanks also to Catherine Low, Charlotte Darnell, Howie, Ewelina Tur, Damon Pourtahmaseb-Sasi, Scott Alexander, Sam Smith, Stefan Torges and the 80,000 Hours team. And thanks to everyone who has written openly about their own mental health. That’s a big factor why people often feel able to ask for help.

One massive thanks to all the EA and AI safety people working on incredibly difficult and pressing problems, wherever you are. Thank you. I hope some of this is helpful. I’m working on more. @Anthropic, @OpenAI and @USgov, I can write more fun blog posts in longer timelines. Pls consider.

And another massive thanks to the operations, HR, and management people at orgs, who make dealing with mental health less of a burden than it would otherwise be. I’ve talked to many of you, there are so many out there who genuinely care and do fantastic work. Thank you.

Special thanks to Nicole, who asked me “please can I just have all your open tabs on EA mental health?” and I said “no that’s not really possible, it’s 600 tabs. But maybe I can make a list” and so now we have a list. And thanks Claude for helping me order my list.

item.title: Recursive Self Alignment: The Model is the Estimator
item.description:
Alignment research has historically been undertaken from the position that we should solve it before the intelligence explosion. But the intelligence explosion has already begun. We investigate what an alignment paradigm might look like in the time of RSI. This is intended to be the first post in a sequence I’m writing.

The model is the estimator

In classical learning theory, learning decomposes into approximation (e.g. can our model represent the goal?), estimation (how well can we infer it from finite, noisy data?), and optimization (e.g. gradient descent).

METR’s October 2026 report argues that the source of recent acceleration is not training scale-up, and attributes most of it to AI assistance. Dwarkesh Patel and Jerry Han argue that pretraining progress has mostly come from data quality, while noting that recent gains have come largely from RL. One can imagine the RL analogue being more interesting here: RSIing on data quality might look like having models remove or fix broken or hacky environments.

So we should expect that during RSI, models are not only making all the small decisions about the training process that might impact the incremental alignment of the final model (e.g. forward KL covering support vs reverse KL seeking modes), but also determining their own reward functions (inferring what the researcher actually meant, given the existing, broken signal, and perhaps some messy feedback, in order to rewrite the training signal for the next run). Thus, in a learning theoretic sense, the model itself becomes the estimator in the meta-optimization process that is RSI, with the researcher’s intended reward as the estimand.

In this paradigm, the model eventually must become responsible not only for estimating reward, but also for applying alignment techniques like CoT monitoring and interpretability.[1]

Incremental alignment wins are often capabilities wins

Prosaic alignment wins found this way lead to capabilities improvements. How? Better environments improve not only specification and estimation (what the RL signal is pointing at) but also optimization (in this case, less noisy and less biased signal). And because the RL signal is better pointed at the objective (solve this coding challenge) rather than a proxy (solve this coding challenge OR reward hack), our process better optimizes for the objective, leading to a model that is both more aligned and more capable, especially per unit time, money, and optimization pressure.[2]

Bias in favor of alignment then amounts to favoring generalization over convergence — getting better at hitting the right target over getting better at pumping more optimization pressure into it.

This is potentially heartening: because incremental improvements to alignment lead to incremental improvements to capabilities, labs have an incentive to build better alignment-estimators and to use them in their RSI loops, which reduces the amount of optimization pressure needed to accomplish any given "prosaic capability". [3]

Now, stopping a coding model from deleting unit tests is obviously a long way from friendly AI. But as RSI moves into messier, open-ended research tasks, fixing broken rewards starts requiring the model to generalize to actual human intent, and I argue prosaic alignment and deep alignment may sit on the same curve, even if commercial incentives don’t follow that curve by default.

By default, however, we should expect that the capability process will likely converge faster than the alignment process (if the latter converges at all), and we have no guarantees about smoothness. [4] It may be important to study ways in which we might be able to empower differential alignment gains over incremental capability gains in this context.

Moreover, this “incremental” frame is worth examining. It falls out, somewhat necessarily. of the learning theory framing, but it draws a throughline between prosaic alignment and friendly AI that old-school friendliness researchers will rightly object to. In the next post, I'll discuss why, in the context of modern LLM training, I think there may be a better chance this path exists than we may previously have thought. I’ll lay out a frame of alignment as generalization, capabilities as convergence, and white-box methods like interp (and methods like CoT monitoring) as regularization.

  1. ^

    To be clear, I'm not necessarily saying that the model is a good estimator by default, just that it is used as one in an RSI loop.

  2. ^

    More generally, not reward hacking makes the model more useful, because it’s more prosaically aligned to what you want to do, and because cleaner training signals are easier to optimize.

  3. ^

    On the other hand, focusing on fewer, less hacky environments doesn't automatically mean less optimization pressure. RL scaling may well be currently bottlenecked on RL environment quality, so fixing them may let labs push optimization even harder.

  4. ^

    That is, we don’t know how the shape of (automated) graduate student descent compares to GRPO, and we don’t have a clear picture of how to apply optimization pressure to teach the model to act on its knowledge of the experimenter.

item.title: To what extents will currently-shaped AI speed up biology research?
item.description:
Suppose that the escalation of AI capabilities tapers off, whether because of strong government regulation or because of technological plateaus. How will this affect biology research? Which sorts of tasks will it speed up a lot, like 10x or 100x or more, and which will it speed up only a bit, like novel experiment design or conceptual understanding? How much will progress toward big technoscientific goals in biology be sped up overall?

I'll give some thoughts below, but would be curious to hear expert opinions.

(I'm especially interested in this as it affects strategy for research on adult human intelligence amplification and/or for strong reprogenetics. I'll include some thoughts on that at the bottom.)

Current-shape AI

By "current-shape AI" I mean AI that has a portfolio of capabilities that is broadly comparable to the portfolio of capabilities of present-day AI. It includes AI systems that are "like current AI systems but more so"—e.g. even more knowledgeable, faster, more reliable, can hold more context, and so on. It also includes AI systems that are "like current AI systems but also trained on X", where X is some mundane thing to expect AI systems to be trained on, such as robotics simulations (as opposed to an arcane thing like self-improvement / machine learning).

"Current-shape AI" would exclude AI using significantly novel architectures or other methods that result in a very differently-shaped capabilities profile. For example, an AI system would not be "current-shape" if it can learn to behave as competently as an adult human on easily-verifiable tasks, using only the same amount and type of data available to a normal adult human over the course of their life.

With current-shape AI, my guess is that biology in general will probably see a modest or medium overall speedup compared to math and computer science.

Speedups we may see from AI

Some aspects of biology research may see major speedups. For example, there may be large speedups in:

  • Literature search. New combinations of methods or information from different subareas that wouldn't normally be tried out (as we've seen in mathematics).
  • Coding, e.g. to implement computational pipelines such as for analyzing sequencing data.
  • Checking and searching relatively well-understood properties of many molecules. For example:
    • Protein folding prediction and design.
    • Predicting interactions between molecules.
  • Operating robots to carry out fairly-stereotyped tasks. These may include tasks that require some degree of local judgement, such as finding items within a sample, adjusting during a multi-step protocol to complete steps properly, adjusting conditions such as temperature as needed to compensate for changes, and so on. For example:
    • Pipetting.
    • Culturing known cell lines.
    • Purifying substances using known protocols.

Things that may remain bottlenecks even with stronger current-shape AI

However, Amdahl's law will probably bite fairly hard. This is especially so for difficult complex goals such as adult HIA: a difficult complex goal will probably require many sorts of operations (experiments, theoretical insights, developing apparatuses and methods, etc.). If a goal requires many sorts of operations, including many difficult operations, then it is exposed to more bottlenecks where it might get Amdahled even if many of the operations are significantly sped up.

In particular, bio research requires mental operations such as concept formation, investigation of novel phenomena, and sample-efficient learning and agency where samples are costly. Current-shape AI does poorly with these operations relative to humans.

Less arcanely, biology is quite different from fields where current AI is increasingly dominant over humans (math and computer tasks). On one hand, math & CS involve tasks that tend to usually be fast, perfect information, well-defined, easy to verify, widely studied, deteriministic, and inexpensive. On the other hand, biology involves tasks that tend to usually have a lot of hidden information, ill-defined, hard to verify, niche (because there are so many different objects of study), non-deterministic, and expensive to carry out. These of course don't pose fundamental obstacles to AI replacing human biologists, but they pose major practical obstacles to current-shape AI doing so. See: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/ocywf8gX9mkNmBxdp/a-wander-through-adult-intelligence-amplification#Appendix__Biotechnology_research_kinda_sucks

Some key inputs to bio progress that we'll get Amdahled on:

  • Procurement. Obtaining tissue samples, culture media and reagents, equipment, robots, and other supplies will be major bottlenecks. It might be possible to accelerate the entire background supply chain supporting biology research, but that is an even larger project compared to "merely" greatly accelerating specific sectors of biotech research. Access to various items may be time-constrained; for example:
    • Human tissue samples are limited, and potentially important for various research purposes. See for example: https://reprogeneticsinstitute.org/articles/Why_better_single_cell_data_about_natural_oogenesis_would_probably_help.html
    • Obtaining, breeding, and caring for animals for model research will take time, resources, and human expertise.
  • Directing cutting-edge research. Even if AI automates large portions of lab work and even experiment design, research strategy and dealing with problems that are hard / ill-defined / complex / etc. will probably require humans.
  • Operations on human cells, tissues, and patients. Biological processes themselves mostly can't be sped up using current-shape AI. Some cell differentiation protocols may get modest speed-ups, but for example animal fetus gestation times, human in vitro embryo growth times, and oocyte in vitro folliculogenesis using ovarian tissue will presumably be largely unaffected. Many experiments and other necessary operations (such as measurements to create benchmarks, validation tests, and clinical trials) will therefore be bottlenecked on serial wall-clock time.
  • Flexible frontier protocol development. Currently, robots are good at doing fairly restricted tasks where there's a fairly clear and fairly fixed set of steps; a robotics setup can be tuned to perform well, and can have some flexibility. With future AI systems, the flexibility of robots will probably be increased. However, frontier research requires trying out pretty novel protocols. For example, when there is a newly important aspect of biological materials to track during a protocol, the protocol has to insert new steps for measuring that aspect and modulating the next steps in response to new scarce information, without a preexisting plan.
  • Incorporating AI into research. Setting up robots to use a new protocol / new devices / new materials will probably require skilled expert human oversight. Using AI for literature searches and molecule searches likewise requires expert guidance and context. Etc.
  • Developing and scaling up suitable robotics.
  • Talent pipelines. It takes years to train up biologists to a level of knowledge where they would be able to direct cutting-edge research. This can probably be marginally sped up with AI, but not by 10x.
  • Building research programs. Fast progress, even AI-powered, will probably require large concentrations of people, equipment, and other resources. Such programs take months or years to build.
  • Interfacing with the world. Working with customers, clinics, regulatory bodies, and the public at large about new technologies will be bottlenecked on expert human work.

Should we just wait and do research later?

Altogether, I expect there to be many breakthroughs unlocked by much faster AI-driven progress in specific areas.

However, both adult HIA and reprogenetic HIA will involve many bio research steps where current-shaped AI would lag, described in the previous section. Those steps would continue to be bottlenecked on human labor and funding. These steps are costly, slow, and have serial dependencies. Therefore they should be started ASAP, not later.

Reprogenetic HIA is, perhaps surprisingly, rather technically feasible. It's so feasible that we may be only 2-6 years from medium-strength reprogenetic HIA (+>1 SDs on intelligence), and 5-10 years from strong reprogenetic HIA (+>2.5 SDs on intelligence). So, much of the remaining progress toward the first strong-HIA babies could occur in the period before or mostly before major AI-bio research speedups. The AI-bio speedup, however fast, can't possibly make strong reprogenetic HIA happen before the fast AI-bio speedup becomes available in the first place. It is feasible to accelerate the last few miles of strong reprogenetics research now, given more funding now. That's a speedup that can't be caught-up to later. Therefore, it should be invested in now.

Adult HIA in particular, on the other hand, is likely to be very difficult. There is no clear technological principle, i.e. no clear way to harness human-intelligence-producing phenomena to produce more human intelligence. There are also major technological difficulties. See "A wander through adult intelligence amplification...". Even with a current-shape AI bio speedup, I expect adult HIA to take decades, say.

Since adult HIA is likely to take decades in any case, it isn't very likely to beat out reprogenetic HIA. Although reprogenetic HIA has an unavoidable delay with helping the situation—at least 15 years, say—this is on the same scale as the difficulty of adult HIA, and reprogenetic strong HIA is close to feasible.

One way the model described here could be wrong: A somewhat plausible scenario for adult HIA would be a large search for drugs that can cross the blood-brain barrier naturally, and that modulate biological pathways in the brain in a way that mimics the affect of many IQ-associated genetic variants. These could plausibly be discovered by AI searches and thinking, and then tested for activity and safety on in vitro neural organoids en masse using AI-orchestrated robotics. See: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/ocywf8gX9mkNmBxdp/a-wander-through-adult-intelligence-amplification?commentId=brmxnR9ajz3pgSRYp. I think this will still be difficult and have serial dependencies (for example, it would require large expensive trials with good psychometrics), but it could plausibly be both feasible and significantly AI-acceleratable.

Compare Hebenstreit et al. (2026) [1] .

  1. Hebenstreit, Konstantin, Constantin Convalexius, Stephan Reichl, Stefan Huber, Christoph Bock, and Matthias Samwald. “What Are the Limits to Biomedical Research Acceleration through General-Purpose AI?” Scientific Reports 16, no. 1 (2026): 1304. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-32583-w. ↩︎
